title: Utility Types and never
summary: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record and ReturnType, and exhaustive switches with never.

steps.title: Utility types
body: TypeScript ships generic types that **transform** other types, so you derive shapes instead of copying them:
```ts
interface Todo { id: number; title: string; done: boolean; notes: string }
type TodoPatch   = Partial<Todo>;                   // every property optional
type TodoPreview = Pick<Todo, "id" | "title">;      // only these
type NewTodo     = Omit<Todo, "id">;                // all but these
type ById        = Record<number, Todo>;            // { [id: number]: Todo }
type FixedTodo   = Readonly<Todo>;                  // every property readonly
type Full        = Required<TodoPatch>;             // every property required again
function makeTodo(title: string) { return { id: 1, title, done: false }; }
type Made = ReturnType<typeof makeTodo>;            // { id: number; title: string; done: boolean }
`typeof value` in a **type position** gives the type of a value, which is how `ReturnType<typeof fn>` works. Derived types update themselves when `Todo` changes.

steps.prompt: Match each utility type to what it produces from `Todo`.
pairs: a dictionary of todos by string key

steps.prompt: Given `type NewTodo = Omit<Todo, "id">`, which value compiles as a `NewTodo`?
steps.explain: `Omit` removes `id` and keeps the rest **required**. A fresh literal with `id` has an excess property; one without `done` and `notes` is missing required ones.

steps.title: never and exhaustive switches
body: `never` is the type with **no values**. After every case of a union is handled, what is left is `never`. Assigning to `never` turns "I forgot a case" into a compile error:
```ts
type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number } | { kind: "square"; s: number };
function assertNever(x: never): never {
throw new Error("Unhandled case: " + JSON.stringify(x));
function area(sh: Shape): number {
switch (sh.kind) {
case "circle": return Math.PI * sh.r ** 2;
case "square": return sh.s ** 2;
default: return assertNever(sh);   // sh is never here

Add `{ kind: "triangle"; ... }` to `Shape` later and `tsc` flags the `default` line: "Argument of type '{ kind: "triangle" ... }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'". At run time, if bad data still gets in, `assertNever` throws instead of silently returning `undefined`.

steps.prompt: A `"triangle"` member is added to `Shape` but `area` is not updated. What happens?
options: `tsc` reports an error on the `assertNever(sh)` line
Nothing until a triangle reaches `area`, then it returns `undefined`
The switch silently falls through to `"square"`
TypeScript adds the missing case automatically
steps.explain: That compile error is the whole point: the compiler finds every switch you need to update.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (Bad data at run time still reaches the default branch.)
code: function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error("Unhandled: " + x); }
try { next("blue" as Light); } catch (e) { console.log((e as Error).message); }
steps.explain: `as Light` lies to the compiler, so `"blue"` gets through at run time. `assertNever` catches it with a clear error instead of returning `undefined`.

steps.title: A new case broke the build
prompt: A teammate added `triangle` to `Shape`. The build now fails, and that is the point of the `never` check:
main.ts(14,33): error TS2345: Argument of type '{ kind: "triangle"; base: number; height: number; }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'.
Make `area` handle triangles (`base * height / 2`). Keep the `assertNever(s)` default, so the next new shape fails the build too.
template: Dojo.eq("rect 2 x 3", 6, area({ kind: "rect", w: 2, h: 3 }));
Dojo.eq("triangle 4 x 3", 6, area({ kind: "triangle", base: 4, height: 3 }));
Dojo.check("circle r=1", Math.abs(area({ kind: "circle", r: 1 }) - Math.PI) < 1e-9);
hints: Inside that case TypeScript knows `s` has `base` and `height`.
steps.explain: After every `case`, the type of `s` in `default` shrinks. When all cases are handled it is `never` and the call compiles; when one is missing, the error names the missing member. That turns "forgot to update a switch" from a production bug into a build error.
